subject: Civil Engineering
title: Bridge Rehabilitation vs Replacement
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Bridge Rehabilitation vs Replacement.

hook.text: Tearing down a bridge and building new costs millions. Can you fix the old one instead?

buildup.text: Rehabilitation strengthens existing components — adding plates, replacing decks.

discovery.text: FRP wraps can double a column's load capacity without changing its size.

twist.text: Sometimes rehab costs more than replacement — hidden damage keeps compounding.

climax.text: Lifecycle cost analysis decides: repair now cheaply or replace once expensively.

punchline.text: The cheapest bridge is the one you never have to rebuild.

quiz.question: What does lifecycle cost analysis compare for bridges?
options: The cost of the bridge versus the cost of a tunnel
Total costs of rehabilitation over time versus full replacement
The cost of materials versus the cost of labor

details.summary: Engineers must decide whether to rehabilitate aging bridges through targeted repairs or replace them entirely. Rehabilitation preserves the existing structure through deck replacement, strengthening, or widening.
details.whyItMatters: With thousands of structurally deficient bridges worldwide, the rehabilitation versus replacement decision determines how limited infrastructure budgets are allocated most effectively.
takeaways: Rehabilitation costs less but may not address fundamental capacity issues
Replacement provides modern standards but disrupts traffic for longer periods
Life-cycle cost analysis compares total costs over the bridge's remaining life

faq.question: When is bridge rehabilitation preferred over full replacement?
faq.answer: Rehabilitation is preferred when the main structural elements like piers and girders remain sound, when the bridge alignment meets current standards, and when the rehab cost is less than about 60% of replacement cost. It also minimizes traffic disruption and environmental impact.

faq.question: How do engineers decide between rehabilitation and replacement?
faq.answer: Engineers compare life-cycle costs including initial construction, maintenance, user delay costs, and expected remaining service life. They also consider load capacity needs, geometric adequacy, seismic vulnerability.
